tr.td: 29 September to 5 October 1944, with the worst killing on 29 and 30 September
The Monte Sole massif between the Reno and Setta valleys, south of Bologna, Emilia-Romagna, Italy
Troops of the 16th SS Panzergrenadier Division "Reichsführer-SS", with some army and air force units and Italian informers
About 770 civilians (the figure NS-Täter in Italien says research confirmed), most of them women, children and older people
Life sentences for the SS major Walter Reder (1951) and, in absentia, for ten more former SS men (2007); none of the 2007 convicts was extradited
The Monte Sole massacre; the "Marzabotto" name is used because most of the places involved belonged to that municipality
The Stella Rossa brigade, led by Mario Musolesi, known as "Lupo"
Described in an army report as a Vernichtungsunternehmen, an "annihilation operation"
Between 1,500 and 2,000 men, according to the NS-Täter in Italien research project
115 locations, from hamlets to single farmsteads
Major Walter Reder (reconnaissance battalion); Max Simon (divisional commander); Helmut Looß (overall command of the operation, according to NS-Täter in Italien)
Casaglia (85 dead), Creda (69), Caprara (63), Cadotto (49), San Giovanni di Sotto (52)
A sanctuary in Marzabotto (set up in 1961); the Monte Sole historical park (founded 1989); a Monte Sole peace foundation (2002)

li.a: World Socialist Web Site: Former SS officers sentenced for massacre in Marzabotto, Italy
Wanted in Rome: Italy marks 80 years since the Marzabotto Massacre
Viaggi della Memoria: Una giornata a Monte Sole

content.p: Over a few days at the end of September 1944, German troops swept through the hamlets on the slopes of Monte Sole, in the Apennines south of Bologna, and killed some 770 civilians. Most of the dead were women, children and older people with no link to the partisans. The research project NS-Täter in Italien, which documents German massacres in Italy, ranks it as the deadliest attack on civilians by German forces anywhere in Western or Southern Europe. It is remembered as the Marzabotto massacre, although the project notes that this name is geographically inexact and that "Monte Sole" is now the preferred term.

Only two commanders were convicted in the decades after the war, and both were freed early: Max Simon in 1954 and Walter Reder in 1985. In 2007 an Italian military court convicted ten more former SS men in their absence. By the project's account none of those men was extradited or even arrested, and no relative of a victim has received any of the compensation ordered.

In the late summer of 1944 the Gothic Line, a German defensive line in the Apennines, was where the Allies had pushed German forces back to. The Monte Sole plateau, between the Setta and Reno rivers, lay just behind it. Two routes ran through the valleys, the Bologna-Prato railway and a main road, and the Wehrmacht used both constantly, the road especially as a supply route to the front. The mountain above them was the territory of the Stella Rossa partisan brigade. Local people had been joined there by civilians fleeing the fighting and persecution in the valleys.

The Germans believed they faced a large force. NS-Täter in Italien says German estimates put the brigade at about 2,000 fighters, while the true figure was at most 500. It adds that the partisans never seriously threatened the supply routes, and that German sweeps through the area seemed aimed more at punishing the population than at a military result.

Reprisals against civilians came through the summer. According to the same project, 27 civilians were shot on 22 July 1944 at Pian di Setta, Montorio and Monteacuto, and seven more in Grizzana the next day; the victims included two boys of fifteen and sixteen. After a partisan attack on 8 September that killed a lieutenant and a sergeant, fifteen civilians were shot. When the 16th SS Panzergrenadier Division arrived two weeks later, partisans killed two soldiers from a lorry near Marzabotto on 25 September. The project says this strengthened the German belief that the district was dangerous and held by a strong, well-armed force.

The area was under the I Parachute Corps, to which the SS division reported. Instead of the earlier quick reprisals, the corps prepared a large operation for the SS division to carry out. A daily report of the German 14th Army, dated 30 September, called it an "annihilation operation", a term NS-Täter in Italien says is otherwise absent from army papers on anti-partisan actions in occupied Italy. The same project quotes a telephone note from 29 September in which the 14th Army's chief of staff warned that the operation was to follow army guidelines and that there were to be "no abuses". Between 1,500 and 2,000 men took part.

Two assault groups did most of the work. One was formed from companies of the SS reconnaissance battalion under Major Walter Reder, which operated on the Setta side. The other came from the Reno side under SS Hauptsturmführer Franz Schmidt. Other units, SS and army, were to surround the area and seal it off. In the days before, Italian collaborators had gone into the partisan zone as informers. NS-Täter in Italien names Giuliano De Balzo, known as "Cacao", as the best known, and says that two Italian fascist officials, Lorenzo Mingardi and Giovanni Quadri, were convicted after the war of collaborating with the Germans.

The troops attacked more than 30 villages in the first two days. NS-Täter in Italien puts the toll at about 550 civilians on 29 September and more than 100 the next day. The worst killings that first day were at Creda, Cadotto, Casaglia, San Giovanni di Sotto and Caprara. At Cerpiano 46 people were killed over the two days, and at San Martino di Caprara 37 on 30 September.

Writer Jonathan Walker, who visited the area in 2018, describes the SS passing through the hamlets along the ridge and killing the elderly, women, children and priests. At Caprara di Sopra, he writes, about forty civilians were found hiding in a hut and forced into a house. The doors were bolted, grenades were thrown in and the soldiers fired through the doors. The World Socialist Web Site, writing about the 2007 verdict, adds that soldiers broke into houses, schools and churches, and that survivors lived only because the bodies of relatives lay over them or because they managed to hide.

NS-Täter in Italien tries to attribute the killings. It estimates that Reder's men were probably responsible for between 320 and 340 deaths on 29 September, and that another 130 to 150 can be put down to Schmidt's group. The SS anti-aircraft battalion killed about 15 at Veggio and Albergana, and air force troops about ten at Sperticano. The project says the killing of civilians at Sperticano can be ascribed with certainty to Wehrmacht units. For the rest, SS troops, above all the reconnaissance battalion, were mainly responsible. It records that hundreds of men were also taken prisoner and brought to Bologna for forced labour.

The "cleansing operation" ended on 30 September, and Reder's battalion was moved to the front. Killing did not stop at once. On 1 October 45 men were killed by an SS battalion, probably the military police of the division, and 18 people were shot at Ca' Beguzzi on 4 or 5 October by a still unidentified SS unit. About a week later Reder's men returned. Reder stayed two days in Cerpiano, and, with some fellow officers, did further violence to the few survivors, according to the project. After that the plateau became a no-man's-land, with the front line close by and German and Allied patrols moving through it. Many of the dead had not been buried, and soldiers on both sides noted what they saw in diaries.

A tribute from the other side of the lines appears in an account by The Observation Post, a military-history site, reproducing a 2008 magazine article. It says the people of the Apennine towns around Castiglione dei Pepoli gather each year to mark their liberation in autumn 1944 by the South African 6th Armoured Division, whom they credit with rescuing the survivors. The same piece says that a road was named for the division in November 2007. Its description of the killing, which says nearly two thousand people were wiped out by 3 October and that a South African patrol drove the SS off on 4 October, differs from the more detailed reconstruction above, which rests on documented research.

The toll has been argued over since the war. NS-Täter in Italien says the first estimates, from Wehrmacht reports, Allied assessments and early press, were between 770 and 800. A figure of 1,830 was announced at the first memorial event on 30 September 1946. The project says it came from the gap between the pre-war census and the ration cards issued after liberation, so it measures general wartime population loss in the region rather than this massacre. It was nevertheless repeated, including in the Gold Medal of Military Valour awarded to the town in September 1949. Research by the regional committee for the Marzabotto dead later confirmed the figure of 770, the project says, and the Wanted in Rome news site gave "at least 770" in 2024.

Other writers give other numbers. The tour organisation Viaggi della Memoria speaks of 995 dead in 115 places. The World Socialist Web Site wrote of some 800 killed in Marzabotto itself and a further 1,000 in surrounding villages, among them about 200 children. Walker's figure is more than 770 civilians, plus nearly 200 partisans who he says were rounded up and executed. The article published on the 2007 verdict also gives a shorter period, 29 September to 1 October, where most sources say the killing lasted until 5 October.
content.h2: The trials of Simon and Reder
content.p: The first investigations were made by the US Fifth Army's judge advocate, after which British investigators prepared cases for their military courts. In 1947 a British court in Padua tried Max Simon, who commanded the SS division, for the division's crimes in Italy. NS-Täter in Italien says he was sentenced to death because his personal responsibility had been proved, then had it commuted to life in prison in January 1948 and was freed on 30 November 1954 after lobbying by supporters in Germany and Austria.

Reder had been taken to an Austrian military hospital in 1945 and then held in a prisoner-of-war camp. British authorities handed him to Italy in 1948. A military court in Bologna found him jointly responsible for the massacres at Vinca, Valla, Bardine and Monte Sole, the last especially at Casaglia, and on 31 October 1951 sentenced him to life imprisonment. An appeal upheld the verdict in 1954, according to the World Socialist Web Site. NS-Täter in Italien adds that the judicial authorities never charged other surviving company leaders whom it considers equally responsible.

Reder wrote to relatives of the victims in 1967 to ask forgiveness, and they refused. In 1980 a military court in Bari granted him parole from the Gaeta prison. In 1984 he wrote to Marzabotto again, admitting guilt and asking forgiveness, and was turned down a second time. In January 1985, Italian Prime Minister Bettino Craxi ordered his release and return to Austria, mainly under pressure from the Austrian government, according to NS-Täter in Italien. Wanted in Rome says the arrangement followed negotiations among the Italian and Austrian governments and the Catholic Church. The Austrian defence minister greeted Reder on his return, the World Socialist Web Site reports, and the release caused indignation in Italy. About a year later Reder withdrew his apology to Marzabotto and his expression of regret at the Bari hearing. He died in Vienna in 1991, aged 75.

The next prosecution grew out of a discovery in 1994, when files kept in what became known as the "cabinet of shame" turned up at the seat of the military prosecutor in Rome. The first investigations proceeded haltingly. In April 2002 the German television programme Kontraste broadcast interviews with former SS men who had been living ordinary lives in Germany, and German President Johannes Rau visited the memorial at Marzabotto during a trip to Italy. Italian and German prosecutors both responded. In Italy, military prosecutor Marco De Paolis assembled a team of Italian police officers, carabinieri and customs officers led by an army colonel.

The trial opened on 8 February 2006 in La Spezia against 17 accused former members of the SS division, none of them present. Because of the crowds of onlookers, it was held in a cinema. After 23 days De Paolis asked on 10 January 2007 for 15 life sentences and the families' lawyers sought 100 million euros. On 13 January the court under Judge Vincenzo Santoro sentenced ten men to life imprisonment and acquitted seven. The World Socialist Web Site listed the ten as Paul Albers, Josef Baumann, Hubert Bichler, Max Roithmeier, Max Schneider, Heinz Fritz Traeger, Georg Wache, Helmut Wulf, Adolf Schneider and Kurt Spieler, and reported the 100 million euro compensation order. A member of the relatives' association said after the verdict: "Justice has prevailed at last. We waited for decades for this verdict." Ferruccio Laffi, who lost 14 relatives, said "Justice was carried out, at least a little bit." The report judged the sentence largely symbolic, since all the men lived in Germany and were unlikely to be extradited.

On 7 May 2008 the military appeals court in Rome acquitted Spieler for lack of evidence and annulled the case against Wache, who had died. It found Kusterer, acquitted at first instance, guilty. A separate German inquiry, which Ludwigsburg investigators passed to the Munich prosecutor's office in February 2003, was closed on 27 April 2009, because the evidence was thin and thought insufficient to bring charges.

Victims were first buried in mass graves, then in small cemeteries, and finally reburied together in a sanctuary in the main square of Marzabotto, which opened in 1961. A memorial church in the town records the known victims with photographs, Walker says, while the ruins of the abandoned hamlets stand on the mountain above. The Emilia-Romagna region created the Monte Sole historical park in 1989, intending to spread what it called a culture of peace. A peace foundation followed in 2002, and a survivors' and relatives' association was formed in 2006.

West German and German officials long stayed away, in part, NS-Täter in Italien suggests, because the massacre was tied to the partisan movement and so to Italy's Communist Party. That began to change around 1998. Rau, with Italian President Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, asked forgiveness in the name of the German people in April 2002, the first visit to the site by a high West German official, according to the project. On the eightieth anniversary, in September 2024, Italian President Sergio Mattarella and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier attended a ceremony in Monte Sole park. Steinmeier called the massacre "one of the many crimes of the SS and Wehrmacht committed in Italy". Cardinal Matteo Zuppi celebrated a memorial Mass in the Marzabotto church, whose crypt holds the remains of the 770 civilians.
The most comprehensive reconstruction, NS-Täter in Italien says, is Paolo Pezzino and Luca Baldissara's Il massacro: Guerra ai civili a Monte Sole, published in 2009.
